Living Well / Free resources

Wisdom traditions & religious literacy

A useful way in

Choose one place to begin.

Encounter particular traditions in context, alongside tools for understanding religious diversity and interpretation.

Spiritual curiosity can become more respectful when it learns the context of the words it borrows. These starting points include academic orientation and resources produced within particular traditions. They are different kinds of reading, and their perspectives are identified rather than blended into universal advice.

Start with: Religious literacy: a starting point. Read the definition and use it to frame one question about context in a tradition you are exploring.

Contextual introduction · Free to browse

Religious literacy: a starting point

Harvard Divinity School, Religion and Public Life

A way to approach religion as something internally diverse and connected with culture, rather than a set of interchangeable quotations.

Begin here: Read the definition and use it to frame one question about context in a tradition you are exploring.

Access: The introductory explanation is free to read; degree programs and other offerings are separate.

Perspective: Academic religious literacy

Explore Religious literacy: a starting point

Context & source

An academic method for learning about religion, not a recommendation to adopt a belief.

Texts and introductions · Free to browse

Access to Insight

Barre Center for Buddhist Studies

A text-focused route into Theravada Buddhist teachings, with introductions and translator information available alongside the material.

Begin here: Start with “What is Theravada Buddhism?” before browsing individual texts.

Access: Public readings and translations. This is an archival collection, not a current course or event directory.

Perspective: Theravada Buddhist texts and interpretation

Context & source

One Buddhist tradition and a selection of translations, not a representation of every Buddhist community.

Texts and commentary · Free to browse

Sefaria: a library of Jewish texts

Sefaria

A way to encounter Jewish texts together with commentary and differences of interpretation, rather than isolated sayings.

Begin here: Choose the Jewish Thought collection or a topic, and inspect the translation and commentary context.

Access: The library can be browsed without payment. Accounts support additional participation and personal features.

Perspective: Jewish textual learning

Explore Sefaria: a library of Jewish texts

Context & source

Translation availability varies; a selected text is not a statement of consensus across Jewish traditions.

Texts and audio · Free to browse

Quran.com: reading and translations

Quran Foundation

An introduction to reading a specific Islamic text with translation choices and explanatory material visible.

Begin here: Read the About page and choose a translation before opening a passage.

Access: The provider offers the Quran, translations, and recitations free of charge. Personal features may use an account.

Perspective: Islamic text and interpretation

Explore Quran.com: reading and translations

Context & source

Translations and commentary are interpretations. This is a tradition-specific resource, not a comparative survey.

BibleProject: visual introductions

BibleProject

A visual way into biblical themes and literary structure for readers interested in Christian interpretation.

Begin here: Choose the “How to Read the Bible” series and start with its overview.

Access: The selected video collection is free to browse and watch; media playback needs a compatible connection and browser.

Perspective: Christian theological interpretation

Deeper philosophy · Free to browse

Religious experience: philosophical questions

Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

A substantial reference for separating a reported experience from the arguments made about its meaning and explanation.

Begin here: Read the introduction and contents first, then choose one question rather than reading every section.

Access: Public scholarly reference; no subscription required.

Perspective: Academic philosophical analysis

Context & source

Keep the context

Take what is useful, thoughtfully.

This is a selective introduction, not a complete map of religions or a statement of Nolan’s religious identity. Traditions contain internal differences, and translations involve interpretation. Read introductory context before extracting a quotation or practice. Inclusion makes a resource available for exploration; it does not imply affiliation or agreement with every teaching.

Selections are based on public source review, not a claim that Nolan uses every resource or belongs to the organizations listed.
